results.title: DigitalOcean raises H100 rental prices 30% • The Weighted Average
results.author: Stephen Van Tran
highlights:
# DigitalOcean raises H100 rental prices 30%

08/02/26, 09:24 AM

DigitalOcean raised on-demand H100 GPU Droplet pricing 30%, from $3.39 to $4.41 per GPU-hour, while H200 pricing climbed from $3.44 to $4.47 on August 1. The provider’s pricing notice attributes the increases to strong demand, and its live GPU rate card lists the new prices; an eight-H100 workload running continuously now costs about $71,500 more per year. Operators should file the move beside China’s 34% AI-cloud price hike: capacity competition can overwhelm nominal model-efficiency gains, so infrastructure quotes need expiry dates in production budgets.

results.title: AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks Price Hike: Up 20% in 2026
results.author: Sofia Lindström
highlights:
# AWS EC2 Capacity Blocks Price Hike: July’s 20% Was One of Four Rises in 2026

- Sofia Lindström
- August 1, 2026
- Cloud Computing

 Sofia Lindström August 1, 2026 8 min read

AWS raised the hourly rates of EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML by roughly 20% in July 2026, across six instance families (P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en and P4de), and the fourth rise of the year followed: on October 7, 2026 AWS raised the rates again, by 15% on most families, so that on eCorpIT’s page, read on November 2, 2026, P6-B300 bills at $16.146 per accelerator-hour outside GovCloud, up from $14.04 in July. The scope is Capacity Blocks, which AWS’s EC2 pricing page describes as a way to reserve GPU instances in advance for ML workloads. The July start date is reported two ways: AWS notified customers on June 26 of a July 1 start (TECHi), while eCorpIT says AWS’s own revised notice moved it to July 7. eCorpIT reports that AWS says the next update is due in January 2027.

## Four rises in 2026, and where July’s 20% falls

According to eCorpIT, AWS made the July change on its pricing page without a blog post or customer advisory: the notice and the new rates appeared on the Capacity Blocks pricing page, and the October rise took the same route. AWS’s pricing page is therefore where a change shows up. The four steps eCorpIT lists, plus the date AWS has given for the next update:

| Date | What changed | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| January 3 | H200-linked rates up 15%: p5e.48xlarge from $34.61 to $39.80 an hour in most regions, and from $43.26 to $49.75 in US West (N. California) | eCorpIT |
| April 1 | 10% rise on US P5, P5en and P6-B200 rates | eCorpIT |
| July | About 20% on six families; effective July 1 per the June 26 notice, July 7 per AWS’s revised notice | TECHi, eCorpIT |
| October 7 | 15% on most families, about 26.5% on P5 and P5en outside the US | eCorpIT |
| January 2027 | Next update due, as AWS states it | eCorpIT |

The steps compound, so the total is larger than any single headline. TECHi puts January plus July at roughly 38% since December. VentureBeat counts four AWS Capacity Block increases in 2026. October lifts the total further, as the single-instance series below shows.

## Family by family: the October 7 rates

The table lists the October 7 rate per accelerator-hour for each family, as eCorpIT reports the schedule. eCorpIT’s page, read on November 2, 2026, says AWS now lists one Capacity Block rate across regions, apart from GovCloud on P6, and puts P5 at $5.970 per accelerator-hour in all listed regions. AWS’s own Capacity Blocks pricing page also lists P4d, which is not among the six July families, at $1.696 per accelerator-hour for standard AWS regions, the cheapest Nvidia family on that schedule.

| Family | October 7 rate per accelerator-hour | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| P6-B300 | $16.146 | Outside GovCloud; up 15% from $14.04 in July |
| P6-B200 | $14.208 | Outside GovCloud; up 15% from $12.355 in July |
| P5 | $5.970 | All listed regions, per eCorpIT; up 15% from $5.191 in US regions and about 26.5% from $4.72 outside the US, July rates |
| P5e | $6.866 | Up 15% from $5.97 in July; used in the p5e.48xlarge series below |
| P5en | $7.895 | Outside GovCloud; up 15% from $6.865 in US regions and about 26.5% from $6.241 elsewhere, July rates |
| P4de | $2.546 | Outside GovCloud; up 15% from $2.214 in US regions in July |
| P4d | $1.696 | Standard AWS regions, from AWS’s Capacity Blocks pricing page |

eCorpIT puts the October rise at 15% on most families, and P6-B300 shows it: $14.04 to $16.146 is 15%. P5 and P5en outside the US are the exception, at about 26.5%. That larger figure sits next to a change in how rates are listed, since eCorpIT’s page says AWS now lists one rate across regions, apart from GovCloud on P6.

Eight accelerators make an instance, so p5.48xlarge now costs $47.76 an hour ($5.970 times eight), and eCorpIT’s own figure for an eight-GPU B300 block at $16.146 is about $129 an hour. Tracing one instance through the steps shows the cumulative effect. The p5e.48xlarge cost $34.61 an hour before January 3 and $39.80 after it, per eCorpIT. Taking eight accelerators per instance, October’s $6.866 makes it $54.93 an hour, which is 58.7% above where the year began and well past the 38% TECHi counted after July.

...

A Capacity Block runs for 1 to 14 days or a multiple of 7 days up to 182 days, with up to 64 instances per block (512 GPUs at eight per instance), and it can be scheduled up to 8 weeks ahead, according to AWS’s Capacity Blocks documentation. AWS’s billing documentation says the block price is charged up front, with the payment landing on your account between 5 minutes and 12 hours after purchase. From the start of the block, the running charge is the operating system fee alone.

...

In AWS’s worked example, a reservation price of $31.464 per instance-hour produced a $6,041.088 reservation charge, and an operating-system price of $1.8432 per instance-hour produced a further $346.52. A budget built from the reservation rate alone comes up short, and the cash for the first line leaves the account within hours of booking.

...

A 30-day block is not a bookable length, so we repriced the same cluster for 28 days, or 672 hours, which is 43,008 accelerator-hours. TECHi’s $539,000 over 46,080 accelerator-hours implies about $11.70 an hour before July. At that rate 28 days costs about $503,000, at July’s $14.04 about $604,000, and at October’s $16.146 about $694,000. The same cluster for the same length now costs about $191,000 more than it did before July, before any OS fee.

## Quinn and Jain disagree on why AWS keeps raising Capacity Block rates

AWS’s stated reason, as eCorpIT quotes it, is that Capacity Block pricing varies with supply and demand and that the adjustment “reflects the supply/demand patterns we expect this quarter.” Two outside voices split on that. Cloud economist Corey Quinn calls the change “a policy decision, not supply/demand”, on the grounds that AWS updated published base rates. Analyst Pareekh Jain says the “most defensible explanation is simply market-based pricing tied to supply and demand.”

The cadence leans toward Quinn’s reading, though it does not settle the question. Four rises in 2026 landed on January 3, April 1, July and October 7, each upward, and AWS has already named January 2027 for the next update. A list-price schedule reviewed each quarter can be announced ahead of time, and AWS’s own phrase “this quarter” fits that reading. Demand is still real, since Jain’s explanation and a schedule can both be true at once, and nothing in the sources rules out another step. January looks like a scheduled review that has gone up every time so far.

AWS is not repricing from a weak position: TECHi reports first-quarter 2026 AWS revenue of $37.6 billion, up 28%, at a 37.8% operating margin. For the hardware side, see our report on Nvidia and AMD GPU kit price increases, and for the capacity behind it our report on data center leases.

## A block is 13% under H100 on-demand list, and the neoclouds moved too

Rank.ai’s November 10, 2026 snapshot lists on-demand p5.48xlarge at $55.04 an hour in us-east-1, or $6.88 per GPU-hour. A Capacity Block at the October 7 P5 rate of $5.970 per accelerator-hour is $47.76 an hour, 13% below that list price. On-demand P5 pricing was also cut earlier: as of November 13, 2026, AWS’s June 5, 2025 announcement says the P5 reduction of up to 45% applied to On-Demand pricing from June 1, 2025 and to Savings Plan purchases after June 4, 2025.

| GPU | Provider and product | Per GPU-hour | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | AWS Capacity Block (P5) | $5.970 | Rate from October 7 |
| H100 | AWS on-demand (p5.48xlarge, us-east-1) | $6.88 | Rank.ai, November 10 |
| H100 | Nebius on-demand | $4.50 | Raised October 1 |
| H200 | AWS Capacity Block (P5e) | $6.866 | Rate from October 7 |
| H200 | Nebius on-demand | $5.40 | Raised October 1 |
| B200 | AWS Capacity Block (P6-B200) | $14.208 | Rate from October 7 |
| B200 | Nebius on-demand | $8.50 | Raised October 1 |
| B300 | AWS Capacity Block (P6-B300) | $16.146 | Rate from October 7 |
| B300 | Nebius on-demand | $9.50 | Raised October 1 |

The Nebius figures come from Sesame Disk, which reports that Nebius raised on-demand GPU rates 17-21% on October 1, 2026; Nebius’s pricing page lists H100 at $4.50 and B300 at $9.50 per GPU hour. The same Sesame Disk report says CoreWeave added a 10% increase after a 25% rise in July, putting its pricing up roughly 37.5% since July. The neoclouds have been raising rates too. For Azure and Google Cloud H100 pricing, see our AWS, Azure and Google Cloud GPU pricing comparison, and for the H200 class on AMD’s side our AMD MI350P and Nvidia H200 comparison.

## Booking before January: an H100 block beats on-demand list only above 87% utilisation

Convergedigest reports that customers pay the prevailing rate when the reservation is purchased, even if the reserved capacity starts after a future price change. AWS’s billing documentation agrees on the mechanics: a search across a range of dates returns the lowest-priced offering available, and once you have reserved a block its price does not change. With blocks bookable up to 8 weeks ahead, a block bought before the January 2027 update can start weeks later at the old rate. AWS gives only “January 2027” for that update, and the first 2026 rise landed on January 3, so do not assume you have the whole month. VentureBeat’s advice is to check Capacity Block rates before buying, since AWS has raised them four times in 2026.

Locking a rate is worth it only if you fill the block, because the whole block is charged up front. A block costs the same whether the GPUs are busy or idle, while on-demand bills only the hours used. The break-even utilisation is the block’s hourly price divided by the on-demand hourly price. For H100, $47.76 divided by $55.04 is 87%, so a block beats on-demand list only if you use at least 87% of its hours. A block also reserves the capacity, so 87% is the cost line and not the whole decision. The comparison sets the block’s reservation price against the on-demand rate and leaves out the separate OS fee.

results.title: AWS raises GPU prices 20% as the memory crunch bites
results.author: Darius Popa
highlights:
# AWS raises GPU prices 20% as the memory crunch bites

Amazon has raised the price of reserving AI chips on AWS by about 20%, its second hike this year. The rising AWS GPU prices show the memory shortage has reached the cloud, where customers have nowhere else to go.

June 29, 2026 - 9:07 am

 

 AWS Credit: Tony Webster from Minneapolis, Minnesota, United States 

Renting an AI chip is starting to feel like booking a hotel in a sold-out city. You pay to hold the room, and the rate keeps climbing. On AWS, it just climbed again.

Amazon Web Services has raised prices for EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML by roughly 20%, starting in July. Business Insider first reported the change, and AWS confirmed it. The service lets companies reserve Nvidia GPUs in advance, so a long training run keeps going instead of stalling halfway.

This is the second increase in six months. AWS had already lifted the same prices by about 15% in January. Stacked together, the cost of locking in this compute has jumped sharply since the new year. AWS said the prices change “periodically based on supply and demand.”

The rise is narrow, not blanket. It hits one purchasing option: the reserved blocks favoured by serious AI teams training or fine-tuning large models. Other options keep fixed prices, AWS said, and the company says it will hold them there. The increase spared Trainium, Amazon’s in-house AI chip, according to The Information.

results.title: AWS Raised GPU Prices Twice in Six Months: What It Signals and What to Do About It - Data Storage
results.author: DataStorage Editorial Team
highlights:
> An AWS p5e.48xlarge Capacity Block reservation cost $34.61 an hour in December 2025. By July 1, 2026, the same reservation costs roughly $47.76 an hour. That's a 38 percent increase in six months, delivered in two separate hikes, on a product AWS customers reserve specifically to guarantee GPU availability. 

An AWS p5e.48xlarge Capacity Block reservation, eight NVIDIA H200 GPUs bundled into a single instance, cost $34.61 an hour in December 2025. AWS raised that rate to $39.80 on January 4, 2026, a quiet, weekend announcement with no advance customer notice. Then, on July 1, 2026, AWS raised it again, this time to roughly $47.76 an hour. That's a 38 percent cumulative increase in six months, on a product enterprises specifically pay a premium for because it guarantees GPU capacity will be there when a training run needs to start.

Two price increases inside six months is not a one-time correction. It's a pattern, and it changes how any organization budgeting AWS GPU reservations needs to plan for the rest of 2026 and beyond.

38% cumulative price increase on p5e.48xlarge in six months Jan to Jul 2026

~15% first hike, posted quietly with no notice Jan 4, 2026

~20% second hike, across the entire GPU reservation lineup Jul 1, 2026

...

## The Two Hikes, Side by Side

| Metric | January 4, 2026 | July 1, 2026 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Increase | ~15% | ~20% |
| Families affected | P5e, P5en (H200-based) | P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en, P4de |
| Example: p5e.48xlarge | $34.61 to $39.80/hr | $39.80 to ~$47.76/hr |
| Advance notice | None, posted over a weekend | Published on AWS documentation page |

The January hike affected P5e and P5en instances specifically, the H200-based families. The July hike was broader, covering P6-B300 and P6-B200 (AWS's Blackwell-generation instances), plus P5, P5e, P5en, and P4de, essentially AWS's entire GPU reservation lineup. Older instance families saw smaller dollar increases but similar percentage jumps, meaning this wasn't a single product line getting repriced, it was the whole Capacity Blocks catalog.

The new July 1 rate card, per accelerator-hour in US regions:

| Instance Family | New Rate (per accelerator-hour) |
| --- | --- |
| P6-B300 (Blackwell) | $14.04 |
| P6-B200 (Blackwell) | $12.355 |
| P5en (US) | $6.865 |
| P5e (US) | $5.97 |
| P5 (US) | $5.191 |
| P4de (US) | $2.214 |

...

Capacity Blocks for ML are AWS's reserve-ahead product: you commit to a fixed block of GPU accelerators for a defined future time window and pay upfront for the guarantee that hardware will be available when your window starts. This is what got the two hikes covered here.

Standard on-demand and Savings Plan pricing actually moved in the opposite direction over the past year. In June 2025, AWS cut on-demand pricing for P5 instances by up to 45 percent, P5en by up to 26 percent, and P4d and P4de by up to 33 percent. That cut is still in effect for those product types.

Put those two facts together and the picture sharpens: AWS didn't raise GPU prices across the board, it raised the price of the guarantee specifically. Reserving capacity ahead of time, the exact thing enterprises do when a training run absolutely cannot slip because hardware wasn't available, now costs meaningfully more than it did six months ago, even as flexible, non-reserved pricing has gotten cheaper over the same broader period.

...

- Two hikes in six months, roughly six months apart, is a rhythm. If AWS holds that cadence, the next Capacity Blocks pricing review would land around January 2027, worth budgeting for explicitly rather than treating as a surprise if it happens.
- The hikes hit reserved capacity specifically, not flexible on-demand pricing, which actually got cheaper in mid-2025. Re-examine whether your workload genuinely needs the reservation guarantee or could tolerate on-demand or spot pricing instead.
- AWS gave zero advance notice on the January hike, posting it over a weekend. Don't assume any advance warning will come before a future adjustment, and don't build a budget that only works if pricing stays flat.
- This is an AWS-specific pattern so far. Whether Azure and Google Cloud hold their reserved-capacity pricing flat or follow AWS's lead is the single most useful signal for whether this is a company-specific margin decision or an industry-wide shift.

...

- AWS raised EC2 Capacity Blocks for ML pricing twice in six months: approximately 15 percent on January 4, 2026, and approximately 20 percent on July 1, 2026, a cumulative increase of roughly 38 percent on affected instance types like p5e.48xlarge.
- The July hike covered AWS's entire GPU reservation lineup: P6-B300, P6-B200, P5, P5e, P5en, and P4de, not a single product line.
- This affects reserved capacity specifically. Standard on-demand GPU pricing actually moved the opposite direction, with AWS cutting P5 on-demand pricing by up to 45 percent in June 2025, a cut still in effect.
- AWS attributes both hikes to supply and demand patterns; cloud economist Corey Quinn has characterized the January move as a base-rate policy decision rather than a genuine supply response. Both framings have real support, and the two hikes alone don't resolve which is doing more of the work.
- The practical response is the same regardless of cause: budget for periodic reservation price increases going forward, separate genuine reservation needs from default habits, and re-run neocloud price comparisons now that AWS reserved pricing has moved meaningfully.

results.title: Reserve GPU Compute Now: Why Waiting Could Cost You 40% or More in 2026 | Source GPU
results.author: Olumide Kingsley
highlights:
H100 rental pricing rose ... On-demand capacity is sold out across every major GPU type.

...

## 1. The Price Move Already Happened, and It's Still Moving

H100 1-year reserved rental pricing climbed from roughly $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to $2.35 per GPU-hour by March 2026, an increase of almost 40 percent in five months. That's not a one-time correction. AWS raised H200 capacity-block pricing again in January 2026, this time by roughly 15 percent, with nothing in the underlying hardware or power cost changing at all. The increase was pure scarcity premium, providers charging more simply because demand for the same fixed supply kept climbing.

On-demand GPU rental capacity has been effectively sold out across every major chip type since early 2026. Teams that already hold on-demand instances aren't releasing that capacity back into the market even as prices rise around them, which means the squeeze isn't temporary friction, it's the market finding a new, higher equilibrium with less room in it than before.

...

The gap between reserved and on-demand pricing has widened into one of the clearest cost decisions in enterprise compute today. Long-term reservations commonly run 40 to 70 percent cheaper per hour than on-demand rates for the same hardware. Where on-demand H100 pricing hovers between $2.50 and $5.00 an hour depending on provider, reserved access to that same chip can bring the effective rate down to $1.00 to $2.00 an hour.

results.title: GPU Cloud Pricing in 2026: Why AI Compute Costs Keep Rising | Aethir
highlights:
1. GPU cloud pricing reversed course: On July 1, 2026, AWS raised reserved GPU rates by roughly 20%, its second increase this year. Two decades of steadily falling cloud prices have gone into reverse, and budgets built on the old playbook no longer hold.
2. The GPU shortage is now a memory shortage: GPU die output has stabilized, but high-bandwidth memory (HBM) is the new bottleneck. HBM capacity sits with a handful of suppliers and takes years to expand, so constrained supply will define 2026 and beyond.
3. Centralized costs hide beyond the rate card: Idle reservations, egress fees, and single-point pricing power inflate AI compute costs well past the hourly figure. When one vendor raises rates, every customer absorbs the shock at once.
4. A decentralized GPU cloud absorbs the shock: Aethir aggregates enterprise GPU capacity from independent operators across 94 countries into one on-demand network.
5. Treat AI infrastructure as a portfolio: Separate training from inference, run agents on Aethir Claw, and consolidate open-source model access through Aethir Mesh.

...

On July 1, 2026, Amazon Web Services raised rates for EC2 Capacity Blocks, its reservation service for AI accelerators, by roughly 20%, only six months after a 15% rise in January. Teams that reserve cloud GPU capacity have watched GPU cloud pricing climb by more than a third since the year began, and AI compute costs are rising across every roadmap that depends on reserved capacity.

Blackwell B300 instances moved to $14.04 per accelerator hour, while H100-based P5 capacity climbed to $5.191 dollars per hour in US regions. These are the most sought-after accelerators in the cloud GPU market.

AWS lifted the same rates by about 15% in January. Repeated increases on flagship instances signal a structural shift in GPU cloud pricing, not a temporary adjustment. Hyperscalers built their business on steadily falling prices as hardware improved. That era has ended because supply is constrained and demand keeps compounding.

results.title: NVIDIA A100, H100, and B200 Rental Prices Rise as AI Demand Stays Strong
results.author: Justin Nelon
highlights:
Rental prices for several generations of NVIDIA data centre GPUs have continued to increase during 2026, challenging the idea that older AI accelerators quickly lose their commercial value when newer hardware arrives.

Market data cited in the report shows that hourly rental rates for the H100 have moved above $2 and are approaching $3, compared with just under $2 at the start of the year. The newer B200 has also increased from slightly below $5 per hour in January to roughly $5.50 to $5.80.

Older models, including the A100, are reportedly seeing stronger pricing as well. The trend suggests that demand for AI computing remains high enough to support multiple generations of hardware rather than shifting entirely toward the latest processors.

...

The B200 currently commands the highest hourly price among the GPUs discussed, while the H100 remains widely used for model training and inference.

| NVIDIA GPU | Approximate January 2026 rate | Recent reported rate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| H100 | Just under $2 per hour | Above $2 and approaching $3 |
| B200 | Just under $5 per hour | Around $5.50 to $5.80 |
| A100 | Not specified | Reportedly increasing |
| H200 | Not specified | Reportedly increasing |

The available figures come from rental market data rather than NVIDIA’s official selling prices. Rates can vary based on the provider, contract length, region, networking, storage, software environment, and whether the GPU is rented individually or as part of a larger cluster.

Spot rental prices can also change quickly when supply is limited or customers need hardware immediately.

results.title: GPU rental prices double in seven months as AI compute demand defies market selloff
results.author: Editorial Team
highlights:
The price of renting a GPU just doubled. Gavin Baker, CIO of Atreides Management, flagged that spot rental prices for the same GPU cluster jumped from just under $2 per hour to nearly $4 over a seven-month stretch, with the observation landing on August 4, 2026.

## The numbers behind the squeeze

Spot GPU rental rates are now running at least 2x higher than contracted rates, based on Baker’s observations from late July 2026.

H100 1-year contract pricing climbed approximately 40% from $1.70 per hour in October 2025 to $2.35 per hour by March 2026.

Baker suspects that spot rates exceeding contracted rates by at least twofold suggests hyperscalers have meaningful pricing power they haven’t fully exercised yet.

## Why GPU prices are rising while AI stocks are falling

July 2026 brought a broad selloff in AI-related equities. But OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and a growing roster of AI companies continue building out infrastructure at a pace that keeps supply tight. Memory supply is expected to remain constrained through 2027, which puts upward pressure on pricing for both newer and older GPU hardware.

Baker forecasts that operating cash flow growth for hyperscalers will accelerate from 31% in the first quarter of 2026 to 50% in the second quarter, driven largely by higher repricing of existing contracts.
